prompt:
A crisp studio photograph, taken level with the base, of a hand-turned wooden puzzle on a craft-fair stall table: a flat base with THREE upright pegs standing on it, marked A (left), B (middle) and C (right).

It carries 5 round disks of clearly different widths -- disk 1 (the narrowest) is red, disk 2 is orange, disk 3 is amber, disk 4 is green, disk 5 is blue (the widest) -- each with its own size number printed large on its face. The stacking rule is the usual one -- a disk rests either on the base or on a disk wider than itself, never on a narrower one.

This puzzle is NOT set up the usual way. At the start the whole tower of 5 disks stands on peg C, widest at the bottom, and it has to be rebuilt on peg B; peg A is only a resting place. Someone solves it in the FEWEST possible moves -- exactly 31 moves -- one disk at a time, always the top disk of a peg, never a wider disk onto a narrower one.

Show the puzzle EXACTLY as it stands immediately after move 21 of that shortest solution for THIS start peg and THIS target peg. Every disk must sit on the peg it really occupies at that instant, in the correct order; an empty peg must be drawn empty.

Keep the picture clean: no move list, no annotations, no captions. The only characters in the image are the letters on the base and the number printed on each disk.
easy_question: Never mind how well it is drawn. Does this picture show a wooden ring-stacking puzzle: a base with three upright pegs carrying round stacking disks of graduated widths? A realistic photo, an illustration, a schematic or a clean diagram ALL count as yes. Answer NO only if the image instead shows just a blank card or plain panel that prints an answer with none of that shown, or shows something unrelated. Answer yes or no only.
